hero.title: Valve Decoder
hero.subtitle: A Python application that turns FlowSafe's historical PDF pick-sheets into a structured, searchable engineering database.
hero.factline: Role: Industrial Engineering Intern · FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions · Continuing during the academic semester

blocks.heading: Problem
blocks.body: FlowSafe's historical shipped-valve records existed only as PDF pick-sheets — a format that's fine for a single job, but effectively unusable as a data source once you need to search, aggregate, or analyze across thousands of them.

blocks.heading: Why it mattered
blocks.body: The facility material-flow analysis needed reliable historical valve-shipment data to calculate accurate travel-path frequencies between facility locations. That data existed, but it was locked inside thousands of individual PDF documents with no structured or searchable form — directly blocking the facility study until a real dataset existed.

blocks.heading: Constraints
items: No clean structured export of the historical pick-sheet data existed — only the original PDFs.
The extracted data needed to be accurate enough to support a real quantitative analysis, not just a rough approximation.
Needed to be general enough to stay useful as a reference tool after the immediate need (the facility study) was done.

blocks.heading: My role
blocks.body: I built the Valve Decoder independently as my project during my Industrial Engineering internship at FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions.

blocks.heading: Data & engineering approach
items: Built a Python application to parse historical PDF pick-sheets and extract structured records.
Processed 19,567 shipped-valve records covering 1,951 unique valve models.
Structured the extracted data into a searchable database, rather than a one-off export.

blocks.heading: Development process
blocks.body: I built the PDF-parsing and data-extraction pipeline first, validated the extracted records for accuracy against the source documents, then structured the output into a searchable database — usable both for the immediate facility material-flow analysis and as a standalone engineering reference tool afterward.

blocks.heading: Solution
blocks.body: A Python application that converts FlowSafe's historical PDF pick-sheets into a structured, searchable database of shipped-valve records — closing the data gap that was blocking the facility material-flow study, and outliving that original purpose as a reusable production/engineering reference tool.

hero.title: Facility Material Flow & Layout Analysis
hero.subtitle: Two years of operational data and a scaled AutoCAD facility model, turned into a quantified case for how FlowSafe's production, cleaning, testing, and storage areas should be arranged.
hero.factline: Role: Industrial Engineering Intern · FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions · Continuing during the academic semester

blocks.heading: Problem
blocks.body: FlowSafe's facility layout — how production, cleaning, testing, and point-of-use storage areas sit relative to one another — had developed over time without a data-driven relayout. No one had a quantified picture of how much material and people movement the existing layout actually required, so there was no basis for saying which layout changes would meaningfully help versus which would just move the problem around.

blocks.heading: Why it mattered
blocks.body: Every job that moves through the facility pays a travel cost between areas — production to cleaning, cleaning to testing, testing to storage, and back — and that cost repeats on every job, every day. Without a quantified baseline, layout decisions were effectively guesses. Establishing a real, data-backed measure of transportation effort was the precondition for making a defensible case for any layout change at all.

blocks.heading: Constraints
items: Had to work within FlowSafe's existing building footprint — this is a relayout study, not new construction.
Had to preserve required adjacencies between production, cleaning, and testing rather than optimize travel distance in isolation.
Recommendations needed to be justified by a quantified model, not intuition, to be actionable for management.
Needed to hold up against two years of real operational variation, not a single snapshot in time.

blocks.heading: My role
blocks.body: I analyzed the operational data, built the scaled AutoCAD facility model, and developed the transportation-effort analysis independently as my project during my Industrial Engineering internship at FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions.

blocks.heading: Data & engineering approach
items: Built a scaled AutoCAD model of the facility covering 104 distinct activity locations.
Constructed the full set of origin-destination travel paths between those locations from two years of production/operational data — 10,816 paths in total.
Applied a distance × movement-frequency transportation-effort model to quantify how much effort the current layout requires, giving a current-state baseline to test future layouts against.
Used the Valve Decoder database to close data gaps in the historical valve-shipment records feeding this analysis.

blocks.heading: Development process
blocks.body: I built the current-state model first — mapping all 104 activity locations and calculating baseline transportation effort from the historical travel-path data — then iterated on layout scenarios, testing changes to production-area placement, cleaning-area placement, testing-capacity allocation, and point-of-use storage locations, recalculating modeled transportation effort for each scenario until arriving at a recommended future-state layout.

blocks.heading: Solution
blocks.body: A recommended future-state facility layout with specific changes to production-area organization, cleaning-area placement, testing-capacity allocation, and point-of-use storage locations — every recommendation justified by the same distance × frequency effort model used to establish the current-state baseline, so the comparison between current and future state is apples-to-apples.

hero.title: Digital Pressure-Testing System
hero.subtitle: A connected digital pressure-testing and reporting ecosystem — from operator station to manager dashboard — built to replace paper-based valve testing with a guided, centrally recorded digital workflow.
hero.factline: Role: Industrial Engineering Intern · FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions · Continuing during the academic semester

blocks.heading: Problem
blocks.body: Valve pressure testing at FlowSafe relied on physical dial gauges and manual, paper-based recordkeeping. Test results — including the three-pop and bubble-test procedures used to verify a valve — existed only as handwritten records tied to a single physical location, with no centralized digital record, no stored pressure trace, and no live visibility into what was happening on the test stands from outside the test area.

blocks.heading: Why it mattered
blocks.body: Every test still required a technician to run the procedure, then separately transcribe results into paperwork that fed the Functional Test Report (FTR) and other downstream documentation. That duplication — testing, then documenting the test — consumed real technician and administrative time on every valve that shipped, and gave managers no way to see test-stand status without physically walking the floor.

blocks.heading: Constraints
items: Had to work on the shop floor, integrated with existing physical digital pressure gauges rather than replacing them.
Had to preserve FlowSafe's existing test procedures (three-pop testing, bubble-test workflows) rather than change the underlying engineering process.
Had to support the existing Functional Test Report (FTR) output that downstream documentation depends on.
Full ERP integration was out of scope — the system needed to lay a read-only foundation for a future Epicor integration, not replace or write into Epicor.

blocks.heading: My role
blocks.body: I developed the system as my project during my Industrial Engineering internship at FlowSafe / Dresser Utility Solutions — from the operator-station hardware and guided testing workflow through the centralized data model and the manager-facing dashboard.

blocks.heading: Data & engineering approach
items: Raspberry Pi operator stations at the test stands, connected to the physical digital pressure gauges for live pressure capture during a test.

Guided, on-screen operator workflows that walk a technician through the correct testing sequence — including the three-pop and bubble-test procedures — instead of relying on memory or a paper checklist.
Every test tagged with operator, job, and valve identification, and its full pressure trace stored against a centralized test record rather than a handwritten sheet.
A manager-facing dashboard giving live visibility into test-stand status, independent of walking the floor.

blocks.heading: Development process
blocks.body: I built the system incrementally on the shop floor: standing up an operator station and gauge integration first, then layering in the guided workflow, the centralized test-record database and pressure-trace storage, and the manager dashboard on top of that same data. Functional Test Report support and the read-only Epicor integration foundation were built to sit on the same central record, so the live test data, the FTR, and the future ERP link all trace back to one source instead of three separate, disconnected records.

blocks.heading: Solution
blocks.body: The result is a connected pressure-testing ecosystem: operators run guided tests at Raspberry Pi stations wired to the physical digital gauges, every test is captured with its full pressure trace and operator/job/valve identification, and that record is centralized rather than sitting on paper. Managers get live visibility into test-stand activity, the Functional Test Report draws from the same recorded data, and the system has a read-only foundation in place for a future Epicor connection.
